attempts.label: DANDI:000218
attempts.paper_title: Routing of Hippocampal Ripples to Subcortical Structures via the Lateral Septum
attempts.entry_title: Routing of hippocampal ripples to subcortical structures via the lateral septum (Tingley and Buzsaki 2019)
attempts.summary: Most findings on lateral septum (LS) high-frequency oscillations held up on the lab's deposited detections: they are shorter and slower than CA1 ripples, occur mostly in NREM sleep and follow CA1 ripples with the reported lag. LS neurons lock to the oscillation trough, but fewer than reported (60.6% against 92.5%), and ripple features predict LS firing above chance, not at the paper's rates. Confinement to LS and stronger ripple-triggered LS firing in NREM sleep did not reproduce; the first rests on site labels that alternate along the septal shank. Travelling waves, depth within LS and optogenetic induction could not be tested, as electrode positions, depth estimates and the optogenetic rats are not in the dataset.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Tingley and Buzsaki (2019) on dandiset 000218, which holds 98 recordings of lateral septum (LS) and hippocampus in six rats, with the lab's ripple and LS HFO detections, sleep states and maze trials. The main notebook uses spikes and event tables (HFO and ripple properties, state dependence, coupling, pair co-activation, reactivation); a second notebook the LFP (phase locking, coherence, HFO power by site); a third the Figure 7E regressions of LS firing on ripple features; a fourth the phase locking of every LS neuron to a site on its own shank. The optogenetic rats, electrode positions and per-recording depths in LS are not in the dandiset.

notebooks.title: Phase locking to each neuron's own shank
Findings of tingley-2019-01 checked on this version

outcomes.statement: LS was recorded in 6 rats with 1989 LS neurons in the phase locking analysis; 62 recordings had a hippocampal population with LS, 37 with CA1 and 25 with CA3; LS HFO rates come from 89 recordings and CA1 ripple rates from 53; recordings held 8 to 74 LS neurons (mean 29.6).
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 1; Figure 1C and 1D legends; Figure 5B legend; STAR Methods, Experimental model and subject details, and Phase locking analysis
outcomes.quote: The dataset used for Figure 6 consists of 62 recordings with both CA1 and LS simultaneously recorded (N = 37) or CA3 and LS simultaneously recorded (N = 25)
outcomes.notes: Animals 6 (DT1, DT2, DT5, DT7, DT8, DT9). LS neurons with more than 50 spikes in high-power epochs (reading a) 1996, within 1989 +- 198.9; all LS units 2551 (reading b). Of 48 recordings with LS and hippocampal units, 38 are CA1 and 10 CA3 by the units' label (CA1 within 37 +- 3.7, CA3 outside 25 +- 2.5); by the ca3_channel flag 29 and 19. LS HFO rates come from 77 recordings with LSRipples and sleep states (80 with any LS table; outside 89 +- 8.9). CA1 ripple rates come from 47 recordings with CA1Ripples (outside 53 +- 5.3), or 55 with ripplesALL too (within). LS units per recording 8 to 74, mean 31.1 +- 15.5 (within). Four of the six counts other than animals are within tolerance under one reading each, the partial bound. Two of the four rest on choices adopted as assumptions (38 CA1 recordings with hpc units as CA1, 29 by the flag; 55 CA1 ripple rate recordings with ripplesALL, 47 with CA1Ripples alone); without either, 3 of 6 are within tolerance, which would be not reproduced. The counts by recording are in the main notebook (claim:dataset-composition).
deviations: Assumed: units labelled hpc are CA1 units, so a recording with LS units and hpc or ca1 units is a CA1 recording. Most hippocampal units are labelled only hpc, while the units of 10 recordings are labelled ca3, so hpc is read as the label of the units not in CA3. The ca3_channel flag, shown as a variant, gives 29 CA1 recordings. The outcome rests on this choice.

Assumed: CA1 ripple rates come from recordings with CA1Ripples or, where it is missing, the hippocampal ripplesALL table, the lab's ripple detection on the same electrodes. CA1Ripples alone gives 47 recordings, outside tolerance; the outcome rests on this choice.
LS HFO rate recordings are those with LSRipples and scored sleep; the earlier LS tables are counted as a variant.

outcomes.statement: Transient 120-180 Hz HFOs occur in LS in each of the 6 animals, with a robust increase in the firing probability of LS neurons at the events.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 1; Figure 1A to C and legend
outcomes.quote: we observed transient high frequency oscillations (HFOs) in the 120–180 Hz frequency range in each animal (Figure 1A, B) and an associated robust increase in the firing probability of LS neurons (Figure 1C)
outcomes.notes: Median LS HFO frequency 142.9 to 149.2 Hz, inside 120-180 Hz in all 6 animals. The HFO-triggered LS spike probability exceeds the random-time mean by more than 3 SEM at the event bin in 4 of 6 animals (DT1, DT2, DT8, DT9) and over +-5 ms in 5 of 6 (all but DT5). Under the five seeds of the random times, 4, 4, 5, 4 and 5 animals at the event bin; the outcome is partial under all. Pooled over 2327 neurons, 0.0072 against 0.0016 spikes per ms per event.
deviations: Events are the lab's deposited detections (claims file, open detail i, reading a), LSRipples and CA1Ripples, whose stored parameters differ from the Methods (LS 120-180 Hz, durations up to 100 ms, peak thresholds of 4 to 6 SD in some files; CA1 130-200 Hz).
The triggered histogram's 1 ms bins over +-100 ms and the comparison windows are those set in the claims file; the random times are uniform over each recording.

outcomes.statement: LS HFOs are accompanied by a suppression of LS firing immediately after the population burst.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph on the local origin of LS HFOs; Figures 1C and 5F
outcomes.quote: LS HFOs were significantly shorter than hippocampal SPW-Rs ( Figure 1F ) and were accompanied by a suppression of firing immediately following the population burst
outcomes.notes: From each event's stop to 50 ms after its time, the pooled probability is 0.001517 against 0.001593 at random times, a difference of 0.000076, less than 3 SEM (0.000201). From 20 to 50 ms after the event time it is 0.001399, below random by 0.000200, more than 3 SEM (0.000178) under the claim's seed; over the five seeds this reading gives suppression under 3 and none under 2, while the window from the stop gives none under all five. Per animal, only DT5 shows suppression, under both windows.
deviations: Assumed: the window from each event's stop to 50 ms after its time, as the reading of the Results' 'immediately following the population burst'. The paper gives no window or test; the claims file names this window and one from 20 to 50 ms, which differ in outcome.

outcomes.statement: Across 6 animals, 29,955 LS HFO events were analysed.
outcomes.source: Figure 1C legend
outcomes.quote: Average power spectrum across all events (N = 6 animals, 29,955 events)
outcomes.notes: LSRipples holds 27014 events in 77 recordings with LS electrodes, in 6 animals (reading a), within 29955 +- 2995.5. Recordings with LS units (reading b) hold 25690. With the earlier LS tables where LSRipples is missing, 28978.
deviations: Events are the lab's deposited detections (claims file, open detail i, reading a), LSRipples and CA1Ripples, whose stored parameters differ from the Methods (LS 120-180 Hz, durations up to 100 ms, peak thresholds of 4 to 6 SD in some files; CA1 130-200 Hz).

outcomes.statement: On average 16% of LS neurons take part in a given HFO, firing an average of 0.23 spikes per event.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 1; Figure S1A, B and legend
outcomes.quote: On average, 16% of LS neurons participated in any given event, firing an average of 0.23 spikes per event (Figure S1A, B)
outcomes.notes: Window start to stop, pooled events: 5.7% of LS neurons fire in an HFO, 0.079 spikes per neuron per event; mean over 73 recordings 6.9% and 0.096. Window +-25 ms: 8.7% and 0.125 pooled, 10.7% and 0.155 over recordings. No combination reaches 16% +- 1.6% or 0.23 +- 0.023. Per animal (start to stop) 3.3% (DT7) to 12.4% (DT1).
deviations: Events are the lab's deposited detections (claims file, open detail i, reading a), LSRipples and CA1Ripples, whose stored parameters differ from the Methods (LS 120-180 Hz, durations up to 100 ms, peak thresholds of 4 to 6 SD in some files; CA1 130-200 Hz).

outcomes.statement: The vast majority of LS neurons (1840 of 1989, 92%) are significantly phase-locked to the 120-200 Hz band (Rayleigh P < 0.05), with a strong unimodal preference for the trough of each cycle.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 1; Figure 1D, E and legend; STAR Methods, Phase locking analysis
outcomes.quote: Across entire recordings, the vast majority of LS neurons (1840 of 1989; 92%) were significantly phase-locked to the 120–200 Hz frequency band, with a strong unimodal phase preference for the trough of each cycle (Figure 1D, E)
outcomes.notes: Detection channel, 120-200 Hz: 1209 of 1996 LS neurons with more than 50 spikes in high-power epochs are locked (60.6%; 52.0% of all 2327). Own shank's channel: 883 of 1129 (78.2%). 120-180 Hz: 61.3%. All outside 92.5% +- 9.25%. The null of 10 circular shifts gives 5.2%. Significant neurons prefer -167.0 degrees, 13.0 from the trough, Rayleigh over neurons p < 1e-300, so the trough preference holds. Per animal 39.3% (DT9) to 76.8% (DT1). Own-shank reading for every neuron: the shanks outside the detection block (own-shank notebook) give 732 of 863 locked (84.8%); with the 883 of 1129 in-block neurons, 1615 of 1992 (81.1%), still below 83.25%.
deviations: The own-shank reading uses the middle site of the neuron's shank; shanks inside the detection channel's 16-channel storage block are read in the LFP notebook (1299 neurons) and the other shanks in the own-shank notebook (1028 neurons).
Filtering is zero-phase (forward and backward), a standard choice; the Rayleigh p-value is the CircStat approximation.

outcomes.statement: LS HFOs are shorter than CA1 ripples from the same animals (27 +- 9 against 31 +- 14 ms; rank-sum P < 0.01).
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 1; Figure 1F
outcomes.quote: These events were significantly shorter in duration (27±9 vs 31±14 milliseconds) ... than CA1 ripples recorded from the same animals (Figure 1F, G; rank-sum test; P < 0.01)
outcomes.notes: LS HFOs 27.8 +- 9.5 ms and CA1 ripples 31.2 +- 13.7 ms in the 4 animals with both tables (DT2, DT5, DT7, DT9), rank-sum p = 1.2e-199; reading (2) gives the same means. Shorter in each animal.
deviations: Events are the lab's deposited detections (claims file, open detail i, reading a), LSRipples and CA1Ripples, whose stored parameters differ from the Methods (LS 120-180 Hz, durations up to 100 ms, peak thresholds of 4 to 6 SD in some files; CA1 130-200 Hz).

outcomes.statement: LS HFOs are slower in frequency than CA1 ripples (147 +- 5.7 against 159 +- 8 Hz; rank-sum P < 0.01).
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 1; Figure 1G
outcomes.quote: These events were significantly ... slower in frequency (147±5.7 vs 159±8 Hz) than CA1 ripples recorded from the same animals (Figure 1F, G; rank-sum test; P < 0.01)
outcomes.notes: LS HFOs 147.6 +- 5.8 Hz and CA1 ripples 158.3 +- 7.4 Hz, rank-sum p below 1e-300 (printed as 0); slower in each of the 4 animals.
deviations: Events are the lab's deposited detections (claims file, open detail i, reading a), LSRipples and CA1Ripples, whose stored parameters differ from the Methods (LS 120-180 Hz, durations up to 100 ms, peak thresholds of 4 to 6 SD in some files; CA1 130-200 Hz).
Frequencies are the deposited peak_frequency values, the lab's instantaneous frequency at the event peak, read as Hz.

outcomes.statement: LS HFOs show no significant correlation between event amplitude and peak frequency.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 1; Figure 1H
outcomes.quote: However, they showed no significant correlation between event amplitude and peak frequency (Figure 1H)
outcomes.notes: Over 27014 LS HFOs, the deposited maximum NSS (peak_normed_power) against peak_frequency: Pearson r = -0.000 (p = 0.96), Spearman rho = 0.006 (p = 0.36), so neither test finds a correlation. The variant peak_amplitude gives Pearson r = 0.006 (p = 0.3) and Spearman rho = 0.020 (p = 0.00095). Within animals peak_normed_power correlates by at least one test in 4 of 6 animals (r -0.087 to 0.124), with signs that differ. The maximum NSS recomputed from the detection channel (LFP notebook, 25690 HFOs) ranks events as peak_normed_power does within recordings (median Spearman 0.877) and correlates weakly but significantly with frequency (Pearson r = 0.081, p = 1.3e-38; Spearman rho = 0.116, p = 3.2e-77).
deviations: Assumed: the amplitude is the deposited peak_normed_power, bz_FindRipples' peakNormedPower, the lab's maximum NSS of each event (claims file, open detail i, reading a, deposited parameters). The maximum NSS recomputed with the Methods' filter (120-200 Hz, order 3) gives a weak significant correlation, so the outcome rests on this choice.
peak_amplitude is shown as a variant.

outcomes.statement: HFO events are seen only at recording sites within LS, not at sites in neighbouring structures.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 2; Figure 2A to C and legend; Discussion, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: We only observed HFO events at recording sites that were confined to the LS (Figure 2A–C)
outcomes.notes: Eight recordings (all DT7) have LS sites and sites of another non-hippocampal structure (acg, cc, ms, sfi). The criterion holds in none. The LS median power ratio exceeds the acg median in all 6 recordings with acg sites, but medial septal sites exceed the LS median in 3 recordings (12.32 against 4.97 in 20170320), and in every recording some site outside LS has a ratio above 1.5 (the largest per recording 3.49 to 44.33). Each recording's ratios rest on 17 to 113 LS HFOs. On the septal shank of every DT7 recording the site labels ls, ms, acg and cc alternate along the channel order, and sites labelled acg or ms between LS sites have LS-like ratios (16.2, 13.3, 16.4 in 20170320) while the acg sites at the shank's end are near 1; without site positions it cannot be told whether the labels or the channel order are wrong, so the outcome rests on the labels. In 20170325 the LS sites' own median is 0.97.
deviations: Power ratios are computed in the two storage chunks (about 14 min each) of each recording with the most LS HFOs, to bound the data streamed.
Sites are placed by the electrodes' region labels; the dataset holds no depth estimate.

outcomes.statement: HFO power and the proportion of phase-locked neurons are highest in intermediate LS and taper towards its dorsal and ventral borders; both are best fit by a second order polynomial of depth.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 2; Figure 2D to F and legend; Figure S1C, D and legend
outcomes.quote: Both the power of HFOs and the proportion of phase-locked neurons were highest in the intermediate LS and tapered off as recordings approached either the dorsal or ventral border of LS
outcomes.notes: The criterion needs each recording's estimated relative depth in LS (STAR Methods, Relative anatomical depth within LS). The dandiset does not store it; its release notes say the relative depth is not in the source files. Session names carry drive depths in um, which are not the paper's depth estimate (implantation depth, daily turns and histology). The per-recording phase-locking percentages it would use are computed in the LFP notebook.

outcomes.statement: LS HFOs are travelling waves, posterior to anterior at 1.01 m/s (4 animals), medial to lateral at 0.53 m/s (1 animal) and dorsal to ventral at 2.19 m/s (4 animals).
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 2; Figure 3 and legend
outcomes.quote: we estimated that the travel speed was 1.01 meters per second in the posterior-to-anterior direction (N = 4 animals), 0.53 meters per second in the medial-to-lateral direction (N = 1 animal), and 2.19 meters per second in the dorsal-to-ventral direction (N = 4 animals)
outcomes.notes: The speeds need the distance between sites along AP, ML and DV. The dandiset stores no electrode positions (release notes: every .prb file places sites by list position with one template), and the probe model of each recording is not stored.

outcomes.statement: The co-activation of LS neuron pairs during HFOs (excess correlation) is not modulated by waking experience on a familiar maze (PRE against POST, rank-sum P = 0.36).
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 3; Figure 4A, B and legend; STAR Methods, Excess correlation analysis
outcomes.quote: It also suggested that the degree of co-activation observed is not modulated by waking experience in a familiar environment (Figure 4B; rank-sum test; P = 0.36; PRE vs POST)
outcomes.notes: Under the 8 normalized readings, the rank-sum test of PRE against POST finds no difference (p 0.50 to 0.89; effect r -0.013 to 0.025). Under the 8 raw-count readings it does (p 0.0036 to 0.0065, POST higher; r -0.10 to -0.12). Only 361 to 503 pairs in 21 to 23 sessions pass the inclusion rule (462 under inclusion a with BEHAV in trials), against 7172 pairs in 53 sessions; no DT8 pair passes. The absence holds under the adopted reading, on 6% of the paper's pairs. The pairs are lost in the HFO epochs: of 20182 candidate cross-shank pairs in 54 recordings, 10823 pass inclusion (a) in BEHAV, 795 in PRE and 954 in POST, 462 in all three; the LS HFOs last 252 s in PRE and 355 s in POST in all. DT8 has 1886 candidate pairs, 3 passing in PRE and 10 in POST. Of the recordings with LS units, 17 have no trials, 7 no LSRipples and 4 LS units on one shank. A variant the claims file does not name, asked of a reader, applies the inclusion rule to all spikes of PRE and POST (CCGs still from spikes during HFOs): 10159 to 15732 pairs in 54 sessions pass, and PRE and POST differ at p < 0.05 in 8 of 16 readings, 4 of the 8 normalized ones (5 ms SD kernel, p 0.00047 to 0.0082; full-width kernel p 0.15 to 0.29), with small effects (r -0.016 to -0.023, POST higher); 73.8% to 76.6% of these pairs have an excess of exactly 0 in PRE. The outcome is judged on the claims file's readings.
deviations: Assumed: the CCG divided by the square root of the product of the two neurons' spike counts in the epoch (claims reading iii). The paper does not say how the CCG is normalized; the normalized reading is adopted because the paper compares excess correlations across epochs with very different spike counts (BEHAV and HFO epochs), which raw counts do not allow. The raw-count readings are shown.

The dataset does not mark PRE, BEHAV and POST. PRE is taken as the recording before the first trial's start, BEHAV from the first trial's start to the last trial's stop, and POST after the last trial's stop (an assumption; the STAR Methods say each recording has the three periods in that order).

Events are the lab's deposited detections (claims file, open detail i, reading a), LSRipples and CA1Ripples, whose stored parameters differ from the Methods (LS 120-180 Hz, durations up to 100 ms, peak thresholds of 4 to 6 SD in some files; CA1 130-200 Hz).
The inclusion rule is applied to the spikes of each epoch (claims reading i); spikes during HFOs are those between each LS HFO's start and stop.

outcomes.statement: Excess correlations during HFOs (PRE and POST) are much greater than chance from spikes jittered by +-200 ms and BEHAV excess correlations slightly greater (P < 0.01), and co-activation during HFOs is higher than during maze traversal (P < 0.001).
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 3; Figure 4B; Figure S3A and legend
outcomes.quote: By randomly jittering each spike by ±200 milliseconds, we found that the excess correlations for HFOs during the PRE and POST epochs were much greater than expected by chance, while excess correlations during the BEHAV epoch were also slightly greater than chance levels ( Figure S3A ; rank-sum test; P < 0.01). This analysis also revealed that during LS HFOs there is a higher degree of co-activation than observed during behavior or expected given LS firing rates (rank-sum test; P < 0.001 for PRE vs BEHAV and BEHAV vs POST)

PRE against BEHAV and BEHAV against POST

outcomes.notes: Under the 8 normalized readings PRE and POST exceed BEHAV (rank-sum p 7e-69 to 3e-129) and PRE, POST and BEHAV each exceed their jittered values (p <= 2.1e-6). Under raw counts every epoch exceeds its jitter; with BEHAV inside trials (reading iv-a) PRE and POST also exceed BEHAV (p <= 4.9e-13), but with BEHAV from the first to the last trial they do not (p 0.13 to 0.87). So only raw counts with BEHAV over the whole span give partially reproduced (4 of 16 readings). Under the four other jitter seeds all 16 readings keep every epoch above its jitter. Under the whole-epoch inclusion variant (not in the claims file, asked of a reader) PRE and POST exceed BEHAV at p < 0.001 in 10 of 16 readings, not in the 4 raw readings with the 5 ms SD kernel (p 0.95 to 1) and for PRE not in 2 full-width readings (p 0.0015 and 0.0021); its jitter part was not run.
deviations: Assumed: the CCG divided by the square root of the product of the two neurons' spike counts in the epoch (claims reading iii). The paper does not say how the CCG is normalized; the normalized reading is adopted because the paper compares excess correlations across epochs with very different spike counts (BEHAV and HFO epochs), which raw counts do not allow. The raw-count readings are shown. For this claim the outcome differs only under raw counts with BEHAV over the whole span (reading iv-b); raw counts with BEHAV inside trials also give reproduced.

The dataset does not mark PRE, BEHAV and POST. PRE is taken as the recording before the first trial's start, BEHAV from the first trial's start to the last trial's stop, and POST after the last trial's stop (an assumption; the STAR Methods say each recording has the three periods in that order).
The jitter moves every spike of the whole train by a uniform amount in +-200 ms before the epochs and HFO windows are applied; one jitter per pair.

outcomes.statement: After controlling for the change in firing rate, by rate matching or by bin size, LS-LS pairs show no fast timescale reactivation beyond chance, and HPC and HPC-LS pairs give similar results.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 5; Figure S2C and legend; STAR Methods, Reactivation analysis
outcomes.quote: When controlling for this change in overall rate — both by down-sampling to rate match ( Giri et al., 2019 ) or increasing bin size — we did not observe fast timescale reactivation of LS-LS cell pairs that exceeded what would be expected by chance, given the observed changes in firing rate ( Figure S2C ). We found similar results for HPC and HPC-LS pairs
outcomes.notes: With 25 ms bins after rate matching EV does not exceed REV: LS-LS in CA1 ripple epochs 0.128 against 0.094 (paired p = 0.23), in LS HFO epochs 0.042 against 0.052 (p = 0.57); HPC-HPC 0.028 against 0.010 (p = 0.18); HPC-LS p = 0.33. The same under four other seeds. The Methods' increase of EV over REV with 1 s bins appears only for HPC-HPC pairs without rate matching (paired p = 0.049). The positive control is weak: without rate matching HPC-HPC EV exceeds REV at 1 s only by the paired test (p = 0.049), so the absence for LS-LS pairs has little power behind it.
deviations: The dataset does not mark PRE, BEHAV and POST. findings.statement: The two rats of the optogenetic experiments (Figure 6, Figure S4), with their light stimulation times and waveforms, are not in the dandiset; its 98 files hold six rats (DT1, DT2, DT5, DT7, DT8, DT9) and no stimulus or optogenetic series.
Electrode positions are not stored, nor the probe model of each recording, so distances between sites, travelling-wave speeds (Figure 3) and CA1 neuron depths (Figure 7D, E) cannot be computed.
The estimated relative depth of each recording within LS (STAR Methods), on which Figure 2E, F and Figure S1C, D rest, is not stored; session names carry drive depths only.
The pre-behavior home cage, maze and post-behavior home cage periods of each recording are not marked; they can be inferred only from the first and last trials.

Most hippocampal units are labelled hpc, not CA1 or CA3, so CA1 and CA3 populations cannot be told apart reliably: 10 recordings have units labelled ca3 and 19 have a ca3_channel flag, against the paper's 25 CA3 recordings.
The 36 units of sub-DT7 session 20170407-936um-1152um-merge have an empty region label.

In three files less than half of the trial time is scored WAKE (DT2 3540um-1288um 20160227, 12.5%; DT5 20161014-1296um-1476um, 20.3%; DT8 20170201-72um-432um, 31.6%), against 100% in the median file; either the sleep scoring or the trial times of these files are doubtful.

The DT9 CA3 recordings (20170518, 20170519, 20170521, 20170525, 20170526) have no CA1 ripple table, although the paper detected SPW-Rs on a CA1 reference electrode for CA3 recordings; DT7 20170410 has 61 LS units but no LS HFO table, and DT2 20160215-122710 has 37 LS units and no event table at all.

The deposited LS HFO detections (LSRipples) were made with parameters that differ from the paper's Methods (120-180 Hz, durations up to 100 ms, peak thresholds of 4 to 6 SD in some files, against 120-200 Hz, 15-250 ms and 5 SD), and CA1Ripples with 130-200 Hz; the files' descriptions say so. Their event counts, durations and frequencies match the paper's (27014 LS HFOs, 27.8 ms, 147.6 Hz).

The electrode table holds no site positions, and the units table at most one waveform per unit (raw_waveform, 32 samples, with max_waveform_channel, in the DT1, DT2 and DT8 files listed; no waveform in the DT5, DT7 and DT9 files). On the septal shank of the DT7 recordings the sites' region labels (ls, ms, acg, cc) alternate along the LFP's channel order, so the labels cannot be checked against the sites' geometry.

Four DT7 files label all 128 electrodes "unknown" (20170327-864um-360um, 20170406-864um-1152um-merge, 20170407-936um-1152um-merge, 20170408-936um-1152um-merge), so their channels cannot be assigned to LS, hippocampus or the other recorded regions.

The lab's LS and CA1 detection channels share a 120-200 Hz signal outside any event: at 2000 random times in 45 recordings the phase-locking value of their phase difference has a median of 0.177 (0.060 to 0.311), against 0.024 with the CA1 phase taken 1 s later and about 0.020 for random phases, and their band-passed signals correlate with a median r of 0.245. The files do not say how the channels are referenced; ref_channel marks the detector's noise channel, not a re-reference.

gone.statement: 25 units in 10 files have spike times out of order (1 to 2782 inversions each), against the NWB rule that spike times are sorted.

outcomes.note: Version 0.250624.0439 held no events, so tingley-2019-01 detected its own on one LS channel per recording, and LS firing at them exceeded random times by more than 3 SEM only in DT1 (6.0 SEM; DT7, DT8 and DT9 below random). This attempt used the lab's LSRipples, new in 0.261110.1911, and finds 4 of 6 animals at the event bin and 5 of 6 over +-5 ms. The criterion's window also changed (+-10 ms summed before, the event bin and +-5 ms now).

tingley-2019-01 measured its own events with a 120-200 Hz filter for both regions, LS 153.6 against CA1 150.8 Hz; this attempt took the deposited peak_frequency of the lab's detections, LS 147.6 against CA1 158.3 Hz, matching the paper's 147 and 159. The lab's LS events were detected at 120-180 Hz and its CA1 ripples at 130-200 Hz, which by itself moves the two means apart in the paper's direction.

tingley-2019-01 found Pearson r = 0.056 (p = 2.4e-47) over 67,186 events. This attempt finds r = -0.000 (p = 0.96) with the deposited peak_normed_power, but r = 0.081 (p = 1.3e-38) with the maximum NSS it recomputed on the same lab events, which would give not reproduced, so the outcome follows the amplitude measure.

Both find no PRE-POST difference with the normalized CCG (tingley-2019-01 p = 0.81 on 106 pairs; this attempt p 0.50 to 0.89 on 361 to 503 pairs). The rewritten claims file adds the paper's 7172 pairs +- 717.2 as an expected value, which 462 pairs miss, so the outcome is partial; the old criterion had no pair count.

The old criterion tested only recordings with at least 5 pairs; tingley-2019-01 had 7, none with p < 0.01, and blocked the claim as untestable. The rewritten criterion drops the minimum and adds 53 +- 5.3 sessions as an expected value, so this attempt's 21 to 23 sessions with 0 or 1 significant give not reproduced. Neither attempt finds both directions.

The old criterion needed at least 10 pairs per recording; tingley-2019-01 had 4 such recordings and blocked the claim (t-test p = 0.81, for the record). The rewritten criterion sets no minimum, and this attempt, with at least 3 pairs, tests 16 to 19 recordings and finds no difference (paired p 0.060 to 0.90). More pairs from the lab's events (462 against 106) also helped.

The old criterion was partial only if PRE and POST exceeded chance up to at least factor 5; tingley-2019-01's PRE did so at factors 1 and 2 only, so not reproduced. The rewritten criterion is partial when both exceed chance at factor 1, which tingley-2019-01's numbers also meet; this attempt's largest factor is 6, partial under either.

tingley-2019-01's own events were not more frequent in NREM than in WAKE (NREM higher in 18 of 49 recordings, p = 0.44), though below CA1 ripple rates. With the lab's LSRipples, new in this version, 72.9% of 27014 HFOs fall in NREM and the NREM rate exceeds WAKE in 66 of 73 recordings (p = 2.9e-12).

tingley-2019-01's detection put 35% of coupled LS events on the same sample as the CA1 ripple, so its median lag was 0.00 ms. The lab's LSRipples and CA1Ripples give 6.20 ms (median of recording medians) and 6.40 ms pooled, with 0.026 of pairs on the same sample (earlier_findings.ipynb).

The old criterion fixed a t-test over recordings, and tingley-2019-01's 0.199 against 0.116 (25 recordings, p = 0.089) failed it. The rewritten criterion also allows the fraction and test over all HFOs pooled, which this attempt adopted (0.302 against 0.091, p = 3.1e-171); over recordings it gets 0.213 against 0.118 (p = 0.0025), which also fails p < 0.001.

paper_notes.statement: Excess correlation (Figure 4B): how is each CCG normalized before smoothing? Raw counts make POST differ from PRE (rank-sum p 0.004); counts divided by the square root of the two spike counts do not (p 0.5 to 0.9). The normalized CCG was assumed. Which pairs passed inclusion (7172), given that the dataset yields 361 to 503 under the stated rule applied to HFO spikes, and 10159 to 15732 when it is applied to all spikes of each epoch?

Which test and window show the suppression of LS firing after the HFO population burst (Figures 1C, 5F)? From the event stop to 50 ms no suppression is found; from 20 to 50 ms a marginal one depending on the random baseline. The window from the stop was assumed.

How was the absence of LS spike locking to individual SPW-R waves tested (no figure or method is given)? Inside CA1 ripples 7.2% of LS neurons are locked (binomial p = 0.012 against 5%); in the CA1 channel's high-power epochs 5.0%. Spikes inside ripples were assumed.
Where do the pre-behavior, behavior and post-behavior periods begin and end in each recording? The first trial's start and the last trial's stop were assumed as the boundaries.

Which amplitude does Figure 1H use? The deposited maximum NSS (peak_normed_power) shows no correlation with peak frequency (Pearson p = 0.96, Spearman p = 0.36); the maximum NSS recomputed with the Methods' filter shows a weak one (r = 0.081, p = 1.3e-38). The deposited value was assumed.

Is the Figure 5E inset fraction, and its P < 6.6e-6, taken over all HFOs pooled or over recordings? Pooled, NREM 0.302 against WAKE 0.091 (p = 3.1e-171); over recordings 0.213 against 0.118 (p = 0.0025). The pooled reading was assumed.

The Key Resources point to github.com/DavidTingley/papers for the scripts that recreate the figures, but the repository (head commit 9f4cd48) holds the scripts of Tingley and Buzsaki (2018) and the network model of Figure 8; the analyses of Figures 1 to 7 are not published.

The HFO band is 120-180 Hz in the Summary and the legends of Figures 1, 2 and 5 and 120-200 Hz in the Results and STAR Methods. The STAR Methods call the 62 recordings with CA1 or CA3 and LS the dataset of Figure 6, which shows the optogenetic experiments, and cite Figure 3B for the state of the phase-locking epochs and Figure 3A for the jitter control of the excess correlation, where Figure 3 shows travelling waves.

entries.title: Routing of hippocampal ripples to subcortical structures via the lateral septum (Tingley and Buzsaki 2019)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Tingley and Buzsaki (2019) on dandiset 000218, which holds 98 recordings of lateral septum (LS) and hippocampus in six rats, with the lab's ripple and LS HFO detections, sleep states and maze trials. The main notebook uses spikes and event tables (HFO and ripple properties, state dependence, coupling, pair co-activation, reactivation); a second notebook the LFP (phase locking, coherence, HFO power by site); a third the Figure 7E regressions of LS firing on ripple features; a fourth the phase locking of every LS neuron to a site on its own shank. The optogenetic rats, electrode positions and per-recording depths in LS are not in the dandiset.
